processes.description: A budget coordinator opens the round by sending managers a budget questionnaire with a return deadline (the first draft of the 2001 budget was due on September 18th). Managers fill in salary, staffing and training figures, sometimes after checking headcount and pay with HR, and send back revised forecasts. The coordinator loads each return into the budget spreadsheets to build the draft; small regions answer briefly, offering a single salary on request.
steps: The coordinator sends the budget questionnaire to managers with a due date for the first draft.
Each manager gathers salary, staffing and training figures for their group, checking with HR where needed.
Managers return the completed questionnaire or a revised budget forecast as an attachment.
Managers send further revisions after reviewing the numbers again.
The coordinator enters every return into the budget spreadsheets to assemble the draft.

stalls.summary: Returns are revised after first submission: a manager reworked the budget after sitting down with HR and then sent a second revised forecast, so the coordinator re-enters figures.

automation.approach: Replace the free-form questionnaire with a fixed budget input form per manager, prefilled from HR headcount and current salaries, that feeds directly into the consolidation spreadsheet so the coordinator no longer retypes returns and revisions overwrite cleanly.
automation.rationale: The work centres on collecting the same salary, staffing and training fields from many managers and keying them into spreadsheets; a standard prefilled input layout removes the retyping and the back-and-forth with HR, while managers still judge the forecast.

work_estimate.rationale: Each round involves a manager pulling salary and staffing figures, sometimes checking with HR, and filling a questionnaire or forecast, plus the coordinator entering the return into the budget spreadsheets. Roughly 60 minutes per return; small regions take far less, revised forecasts after HR review take more. Prefilled HR data and direct spreadsheet loading could take over the lookup and re-entry.

processes.description: An organiser, often a manager or assistant, announces a group, staff or management meeting or asks recipients to hold a date, and asks them to reply if they cannot attend or which of several dates suits them. Attendees confirm or sign up, the organiser collects head counts for catering, books a conference room or sends a calendar invitation, and sometimes chases more detail about the meeting from whoever requested it.
steps: Someone requests a meeting or the organiser plans a regular group meeting.
The organiser emails the date, time and room, or asks recipients to hold or choose between dates.
Recipients reply with availability or sign up for a date.
The organiser tallies attendance and finalises numbers for food or space.
The organiser books the room or sends a calendar invitation and confirms the arrangement.

stalls.summary: Organisers sometimes lack details of the meeting they are arranging and have to call the requester for more information before confirming.
Final head counts are still being collected close to the event, so the organiser keeps chasing confirmations to finalise numbers.

automation.approach: Use shared calendar invitations with built-in accept or decline and date polling instead of reply-to-email availability requests, with a standard announcement template carrying date, time, room and an RSVP deadline so head counts come from the calendar responses.
automation.rationale: Most rounds are a short announcement or a request to hold or choose a date; a consistent invitation with RSVP built in cuts the manual tallying and the chasing, while organisers still pick dates and rooms.

work_estimate.rationale: Hands-on work beyond the emails is small: checking calendars, booking a conference room, tallying replies and finalising numbers for food. Around 10 minutes per meeting, more for offsites or events needing catering counts. Calendar polling and RSVP tracking could take over the tallying.

processes.description: Desk controllers produce the daily position report and P&L for each desk, post the files to shared folders, and answer traders' and managers' questions about moves in the results. Rounds include explaining month-to-date swings, booking prior-period adjustments and liquidations, gathering support documentation for accounting, correcting understated or overstated figures, and restating P&L files. Spreadsheet macros and booklists need refreshing, and system outages delay the report.
steps: The controller runs the desk's positions and P&L from the trading systems.
The P&L file is saved to the shared regional folder and sent to traders and management.
Traders or managers question an unexpected figure or change in month-to-date P&L.
The controller researches the move, checks positions, volumes and liquidation values, and gathers support.
Adjustments or corrections are booked and the P&L is restated where needed.
The explanation and corrected file go back to the requester.

stalls.summary: Spreadsheet tooling breaks: users must edit a copy macro in saved P&L files and refresh the booklist before the reports work.
A system outage stopped the controller from producing the report on time.
Reported figures need rework: a controller caused confusion that had to be cleared up, P&L was understated and later restated, and booking errors needed corrective transactions.
Fixes wait on individuals being back in the office.

contradictions.summary: The P&L figures disagree with themselves: one trader's reported P&L was understated, a reviewer called a result way too high, and a day's P&L was restated with a new final file.

automation.approach: Generate each region's P&L and position files on a schedule into a common posting location, with automated checks that flag large day-over-day month-to-date changes and unbooked liquidations, and a standard explanation template listing adjustments with their support.
automation.rationale: Much of the effort goes to explaining swings and correcting bookings after the fact; a daily close checklist covering saving to the shared folder, refreshing macros and booklists, checking rolled-off positions and liquidation values catches the recurring errors before traders query them.

work_estimate.rationale: A round means researching a P&L move or adjustment: checking positions and net open contracts, reconciling liquidation volumes, gathering support documentation, booking corrections and restating files. About 45 minutes per round, short for a file posting, long for a booking error needing restatement. Automated variance flags and file generation could take over part of the lookup; judgement on corrections stays manual.
